Sing something unaccompanied, with nothing to hide behind.
Learn a song in another language.
Sing three songs from memory, back to back.
Sing something to somebody who needed cheering up.
Lead a song that everybody joins in with.
Get somebody who says they cannot sing to sing one whole song.

tracks.name: An instrument
tracks.line: One note to playing for people.

steps.test: Get one clear note out of an instrument.
steps.note: Any instrument. A tin whistle costs less than a takeaway and five notes gets you a tune.

steps.test: Play three different notes cleanly, one after another.
Play five notes in a row without a squeak or a buzz.
Play a five-note tune anybody recognises.
Play that tune three times in a row without a mistake.
Play a whole tune from beginning to end.
Play a tune in time with a beat — a metronome, or your own foot.
steps.note: In time matters more than fast. Slow and steady beats quick and lumpy, every time.

steps.test: Learn a second tune from scratch, on your own, with nobody teaching you.
Take the bar you keep getting wrong, play it slowly twenty times, and get it right.
steps.note: This is the actual skill, and almost nobody is taught it. Not playing the tune — fixing the one bar. Slow enough that it is never wrong, twenty times, then speed up.

steps.test: Play three tunes from memory.
Practise ten minutes a day for two weeks without missing a day.
Play a whole tune for one person, in the room with you.
Work a short tune out by ear, with nobody showing you the notes.
steps.note: Something you can hum. Find the first note, then the next. It takes longer than you think and it changes how you hear music.

steps.test: Learn a tune from written music, or from tab, on your own.
Play with somebody else, in time.
Play a tune all the way through for somebody without stopping, mistakes and all.
steps.note: Everybody hears the stop. Almost nobody hears the wrong note.

steps.test: Learn the beginner version of a song you actually like.
steps.note: The simple arrangement, not the record. Every song has one and it is not cheating.

steps.test: Play that song end to end, three times, without stopping.
Play it from memory, with nothing in front of you.
Play it for two or three people, and show one of them the first line.

tracks.name: Rhythm
tracks.line: Clapping in time to holding a beat for others.

steps.test: Clap in time with a song, all the way through.
Keep a steady beat on a drum for one minute.
Keep it for two minutes without speeding up.
steps.note: Everybody speeds up. Recording yourself is the fastest way to find out that you do.

steps.test: Clap a rhythm somebody gives you, back at them, correctly.
Clap on the offbeat while somebody claps on the beat.
Count a bar of four out loud while you play it.
Play a rhythm in three, and one in four, and hear the difference.
Play two different rhythms with your two hands.
Keep time with a metronome for three minutes.
Hold the beat while other people play over it.
Stop and come back in on the right beat.
Lead a drum circle.

tracks.name: Whistling
tracks.line: One note to a whole tune.

steps.test: Whistle one clear note.
Whistle two notes, one after the other.
Whistle up and down, high to low.
Whistle a tune somebody can name.
Whistle it in tune, checked against the real thing.
Whistle three tunes properly.
Whistle loudly with your fingers.
Teach somebody who cannot whistle to whistle.

tracks.name: Writing a song
tracks.line: Two lines to a song people sing.

steps.test: Write two lines that rhyme and mean something.
Write four lines about one thing that actually happened.
Say them out loud and cut every word that is not needed.
Write a whole verse.
Put a tune to it, even a simple one.
Write a chorus that says the one thing the song is about.
Sing the verse and the chorus to one person.
Change one line because of what they said.
Write a second verse that moves the story on.
Get the whole thing under three minutes.
Play or sing it the same way twice.
Write it down so somebody else could play it.
Record it, however roughly.
Listen back and fix the one thing that is wrong.
Write a whole song and perform it.
Write one for somebody, about them.
Give it to them.
Write a second song without waiting to feel like it.
Write one somebody else asks to hear again.
Write one the group sings without you starting it.

tracks.name: Reading music
tracks.line: Naming notes to sight-reading.

steps.test: Name every note on a line of written music.
Name the notes in the spaces and on the lines of the treble clef.
Clap a written line of rhythm, in time.
Say the note names of a simple tune out loud, in order.
Play a five-note written line on an instrument.
Read and clap crotchets, minims and quavers.
Play a written line in time with a beat.
Find middle C on a keyboard and point to it on the page.
Play a whole eight-bar tune from the page.
Read the time signature and count yourself in.
Play a tune you have never heard, from the page, slowly.
Read sharps and flats, and play them right.
Play a tune in a key with one sharp in it.
Name the notes in the bass clef.
Play a written line with your left hand.
Play a tune with a repeat, and a first and second ending.
Write out a four-bar tune you made up, so somebody else could play it.
Have somebody play what you wrote, and hear that it is right.
Sight-read a simple tune you have never seen, first try, slowly.
Sight-read a simple tune at proper speed, in front of somebody.

tracks.name: Dance
tracks.line: One step to leading the floor.

steps.test: Learn one dance step and do it in time.
Do it without counting out loud.
Learn three steps and put them together.
Dance in front of one other person.
Learn a whole short dance and do it with somebody.
Hold a frame with a partner and move without treading on them.
Lead, or follow, and let the other one do the opposite.
Dance a ceili dance properly with a set.
Learn a second set dance.
Dance at something where other people were watching.
Keep going after a mistake instead of stopping.
Learn a dance from another country.
Dance to music you have never heard before.
Ask somebody to dance.
Dance with somebody much older than you.
Make up a dance of your own.
Teach it to one person.
Teach it to two people and get them dancing it together.
Get somebody up who said they do not dance.
Lead the dancing at a group evening.

tracks.name: A song all the way through
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One song, sung whole, then sung to somebody.

steps.test: Sing one song all the way through with somebody singing beside you.
Sing it all the way through on your own, with nobody helping.
Sing it without forgetting any of the words.
Clap the beat while somebody else sings it.
Sing it and clap the beat at the same time.
Sing it as loud as you can.
Sing it so quietly that only the person next to you can hear.
Sing it fast, then sing it slow.
Sing it to somebody who has never heard you sing it.
Learn a second song all the way through.
Make up a new verse and sing that too.
Sing your song to a whole roomful of people.

categories.name: Magic and performance
categories.line: Card tricks, coins, sleight of hand, mind reading, mime, puppets.

tracks.name: Card tricks
tracks.line: One trick to a whole act.

steps.test: Do one card trick that works, on one person.
steps.note: A self-working one out of a book counts. Start where it cannot go wrong.

steps.test: Do the same trick three times without fumbling it.
Shuffle a deck properly, twice, without dropping any.
Cut the deck one-handed.
Learn a false cut that looks like a real one.
Force a card so the person is sure they chose freely.
Control a chosen card to the top of the deck.
Do a trick that genuinely fools an adult.
Do a trick and never say what is about to happen.
steps.note: Announcing it gives them somewhere to look. Say nothing and they cannot follow the method.

steps.test: Learn a double lift.
Do three tricks in a row without a mistake.
Do a trick with the cards in somebody else's hands.
Do one with a deck that is not yours.
Do a trick with your own patter, in your own words.
Do one where you never touch the cards at all.
Perform to four people standing around you.
Have a trick go wrong and finish anyway.
Build a routine where each trick leads into the next.
Perform a five-minute card act for a group.
Teach somebody one trick until they can fool a third person with it.

tracks.name: Coin tricks
tracks.line: Vanishing one to the whole routine.

steps.test: Make a coin vanish and reappear.
Palm a coin and let somebody look at your hand.
Do a French drop so nobody sees it.
Do it slowly enough that it looks natural.
steps.note: Speed hides nothing. What hides it is doing the fake exactly like the real thing.

steps.test: Look at your empty hand, not at the hand with the coin.
Vanish a coin and show both hands empty.
Produce a coin from behind somebody's ear convincingly.
Make a coin travel from one hand to the other.
Do three coin moves in one routine.
Do a routine with a borrowed coin.
Make a coin go through a table.
Do a routine with your own patter.
Do it standing, with people close.
Do it surrounded, with people watching from all sides.
Vanish four coins one at a time.
End on a production of something bigger than a coin.
Perform it twice in a row to the same person without them catching it.
Do a coin routine for a group.
Keep the method to yourself when somebody asks.
Teach somebody the French drop until they can fool you.

tracks.name: Mind reading
tracks.line: One guess to a proper effect.

steps.test: Do a trick where you name a card somebody chose.
Do it without saying how clever it was.
Do one that works on two people in a row.
Learn to force a word or a number.
Do a prediction you wrote before they chose.
Read somebody's body language and guess right three times.
Ask a question that tells you the answer without them noticing.
Do an effect where you never touch anything.
Take longer over it than feels comfortable.
steps.note: Mind reading that is instant looks like a trick. Mind reading that seems to cost you something looks real.

steps.test: Get one wrong on purpose and then get it right.
Do a full mind reading effect with a story around it.
Do it on somebody who came in wanting to catch you.
Do one where the method is invisible even on a second showing.
Say plainly that it is a trick, and still have it land.
Do one that uses something of theirs.
Do a two-person effect with somebody helping you.
Perform three effects to a group and keep the method secret.
Take a guess with nothing to fall back on, and be wrong gracefully.
Build a ten-minute set that builds to one big finish.
Never use it to make somebody feel foolish.

tracks.name: Mime and clowning
tracks.line: One gesture to holding a room silently.

steps.test: Mime one action so clearly that somebody names it.
Mime three in a row and have all three named.
Do the invisible wall convincingly.
Do the rope pull.
Keep the wall in exactly the same place for a whole minute.
steps.note: The whole illusion is that the invisible thing does not move. One slip and it is gone.

steps.test: Mime carrying something heavy, then something light.
Tell a whole tiny story with no words.
Make somebody laugh without saying anything.
Mime a whole conversation with a person who is not there.
Do a walking-on-the-spot walk.
Perform a two-minute silent piece.
Run a mime game for younger children.

tracks.name: Puppets
tracks.line: Making one to putting on a show.

steps.test: Make a puppet out of a sock or a paper bag.
Give it a voice and keep the voice the same for two minutes.
Make it look at things, and at people.
steps.note: Where the puppet looks is what makes it alive. Nothing else comes close.

steps.test: Make it breathe while it is not talking.
Have it talk to one person and get an answer.
Make a puppet with moving parts.
Make a second puppet with a different voice.
Have the two of them talk to each other.
Write a short puppet story with a beginning and an end.
Perform it to two people.
Build a stage and run a proper show.
Run a puppet show younger children ask for again.

tracks.name: Circus skills
tracks.line: Spinning a plate to a routine.

steps.test: Spin a plate or a hoop and keep it going for ten seconds.
Keep it going for thirty seconds.
Keep a hoop spinning round your waist for thirty seconds.
Get a diabolo or devil sticks going at all.
Keep a diabolo or devil sticks going for thirty seconds.
Keep it going for a whole minute.
Do ten keepy-uppies with a football.
Do twenty-five keepy-uppies.
Spin a hoop on your arm and move it to the other arm.
Learn one trick with clubs, poi or a hoop.
Do that trick five times out of five.
Learn a second trick.
Throw and catch one club.
Learn a trick that goes wrong in front of people and recover from it.
Put two tricks together without stopping in between.
Put three circus tricks into one routine.
Do the routine to music, in time.
Perform it to five people.
Perform your routine at a day out.
Teach somebody their first trick until they can do it on their own.

categories.name: Food and the kitchen
categories.line: Knife skills, cooking, baking, growing, preserving, hosting.

tracks.name: Knife and board
tracks.line: Buttering bread to teaching a younger one.

steps.test: Butter a slice of bread properly, right to the edges.
Spread something soft on a cracker without breaking it.
Cut a soft thing — a banana, a mushroom — with a table knife.
Learn the claw grip, with your fingertips tucked under.
steps.note: Curled knuckles guide the blade. Flat fingers are how everybody cuts themselves.

steps.test: Peel a vegetable without taking half of it away.
Chop safely, sitting down, with an adult beside you.
Cut a flat side on a round vegetable first so it cannot roll.
Chop an onion without help.
Cut everything for one dish to roughly the same size.
Prepare all the vegetables for a whole meal.
Sharpen a knife and cut with it before and after.
Teach a younger child to chop safely.

tracks.name: Cooking a meal
tracks.line: Cold breakfast to feeding the group.

steps.test: Make yourself a cold breakfast and clear it away.
Make a hot drink safely.
Boil an egg the way you like it.
Make beans on toast, both parts ready at once.
Read a recipe all the way through before you start.
steps.note: Half of all kitchen disasters are somebody finding out on page two what they needed on page one.

steps.test: Get everything out and weighed before the pan goes on.
Cook pasta and a sauce and get them together hot.
Cook a hot meal for yourself.
Fry something without burning it or leaving it raw.
Taste as you go and change it — more salt, more acid.
Cook a hot meal for your family.
Cook the same meal again, better.
Cook a meal from what happened to be in the house.
Time three things so they are all ready together.
Cook a roast, with the vegetables.
Cook for somebody with something they cannot eat, and get it right.
Clean as you go, so the kitchen is nearly clear when you sit down.
Cook three courses and get them on the table hot.
Cook for eight people.
Cook for the whole group at a day out.

tracks.name: Baking
tracks.line: Weighing to selling.

steps.test: Weigh ingredients accurately on a scale.
Bake something from a packet mix, exactly as it says.
Bake something by following a recipe on your own.
Rub butter into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs.
Make scones or shortbread that come out right.
Line and grease a tin so nothing sticks.
Bake a sponge that rises.
Know when something is done without cutting it open.
Bake something twice and make the second one better.
Make a dough and knead it for ten full minutes.
Make a loaf of bread from flour and water.
Make one where the crumb is even all the way through.
Bake something with a filling that does not leak.
Ice or decorate something so it looks like it was meant to.
Bake something without looking at the recipe.
Bake for somebody's birthday.
Bake to order for somebody else, to what they asked for.
Work out what a batch costs you to make.
Price it and sell what you baked to people who are not related to you.
Teach somebody to bake one thing, start to finish, hands off.

tracks.name: Cooking on fire
tracks.line: Toast on a stick to a whole meal outdoors.

steps.test: Toast something on a stick over a fire and eat it.
Wait for embers instead of cooking on flames.
steps.note: Flames burn the outside and leave the middle raw. Embers are what you actually cook on.

steps.test: Cook an egg or a sausage over a fire without burning it.
Bake a bread twist on a stick.
Wrap something in foil and cook it in the embers.
Keep a fire steady at cooking heat for twenty minutes.
Cook a one-pot meal over a fire for two people.
Set up a pot so it hangs or stands steady over the heat.
Cook two things at once over the same fire.
Wash up outdoors and leave no trace of any of it.
Cook a full meal outdoors for six.
Run the fire and the food for a whole day out.

tracks.name: Growing
tracks.line: One seed to feeding people.

steps.test: Plant a seed and keep it alive for a month.
Water it without drowning it, and say how you knew.
Grow something fast — cress, radishes — and eat it.
Grow something you then eat, that took longer than a month.
Find out what your soil is like and what suits it.
Dig a bed or fill a pot properly and plant it out.
Sow seed in a tray and prick the seedlings out.
Keep a patch weeded every week for a month.
Lose a crop, work out why, and say what you would do differently.
steps.note: Everybody who grows anything kills things. The ones who get good are the ones who work out why.

steps.test: Grow three different things through a whole season.
Harvest something at the right moment, not too early or too late.
Grow something from a cutting rather than a seed.
Make compost and put it back on the ground.
Grow something over winter.
Save seed and grow next year's from it.
Grow enough of one thing to make a whole meal from it.
Grow enough to give some away.
Keep a note through a season of what worked and what did not.
Plant something that will not be ready for a year.
Run a growing patch for the group.

tracks.name: Keeping food
tracks.line: Jam to a full store cupboard.

steps.test: Make jam that sets.
Sterilise the jars properly before you fill them.
Label and date everything you put away.
Make a second batch that sets better than the first.
Pickle something in vinegar.
Eat it a month later and say whether it worked.
Freeze a harvest so it is still good in three months.
Dry herbs or fruit until they keep.
Make a chutney.
Ferment something — sauerkraut, kefir, a sourdough starter.
Keep a starter or a ferment alive for a month.
Salt or cure something.
Bake with something you preserved yourself.
Cook a whole meal using three things you put away.
Preserve a glut that would otherwise have been thrown out.
Fill a shelf with things you made that keep.
Know which of them is safe how long, and why.
Throw out something that went wrong, without arguing with yourself.
Give away a box of it and have people ask for more.
Teach somebody to make one thing that keeps.

tracks.name: Feeding people
tracks.line: Laying a table to hosting an evening.

steps.test: Lay a table properly for everybody.
Put something on the table that nobody asked for — flowers, a candle.
Serve a meal and make sure everybody has what they need.
Ask everybody what they cannot eat, before you plan anything.
Plan a meal for six on paper before cooking it.
Write the timings backwards from when you want to sit down.
steps.note: Start from the moment the plates hit the table and work back. Everything else is guessing.

steps.test: Cook something the day before so there is less to do on the day.
Get everybody sitting down within ten minutes of when you said.
Introduce two guests to each other with something they have in common.
Notice the person saying least, and bring them in.
Cook and host a meal for people who are not family.
Do it to a budget and come in under.
Have something go wrong and say nothing about it.
Feed somebody who turned up unexpectedly.
Host somebody new to the area, on their own.
Get somebody else to help, and let them do it their way.
Host an evening with a reason to it — a birthday, a leaving, a welcome.
Sit down and eat with them instead of hovering in the kitchen.
Send everybody home with something.
Host an evening people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: In the kitchen
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Hands washed, then stirring, spreading, cracking and making.

steps.test: Wash your hands properly before you touch any food.
Put an apron on by yourself.
Stir something in a bowl until it is all mixed and nothing is left at the bottom.
Pour from a small jug into a bowl without spilling it.
Spread butter on a slice of bread, right to the edges, without tearing it.
Peel a banana or a satsuma all by yourself.
Crack an egg into a bowl.
Pick the bits of shell out.
Weigh something on the scales and say the number.
Make a sandwich and give it to somebody to eat.
Wipe the table and put your things in the sink afterwards.
Help make one whole thing for everybody's tea.

categories.name: Money and business
categories.line: Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.

tracks.name: Handling money
tracks.line: Naming coins to a weekly shop.

steps.test: Name every coin and note when somebody holds one up.
Count out one pound in three different ways.
Work out what two things cost together, before the till says.
Pay for something yourself and check the change is right.
Say what something costs in a whole hour of somebody working.
Give correct change from a five-pound note, five times running.
Compare two sizes of the same thing and say which is better value.
Write down every penny you spend for one week.
Look at that week and say where it actually went.
Keep a written record of money in and out for a month, and balance it.
Plan a week's shopping on paper with a budget on it.
Do a full weekly shop to that budget and come in under it.

tracks.name: Earning
tracks.line: One job to paying somebody else.

steps.test: Do one real job and be paid for it.
Agree what the job is and what it pays, before you start.
steps.note: Agreeing afterwards is how people end up feeling cheated on both sides.

steps.test: Finish it properly even though nobody was watching.
Do a job for somebody outside your own family.
Ask somebody if they need anything done.
Do the same job for the same person twice.
Turn up on time, three times running.
Say how much you charge, out loud, without apologising for it.
Do a job badly, own it, and put it right for nothing.
Hold a paid job around the place for a season, and turn up for it.
Save half of everything you earn for a month.
Work out what an hour of your time is worth right now.
Turn ten pounds into thirty pounds honestly, and show your working.
Find a second way of earning that is not selling your hours.
Get somebody to come back to you because of the last job.
Ask for more than you asked last time, and get it.
Turn down a job that was not worth doing.
Get somebody else a job you could not do.
Pay another person a fair share for their part in something you ran.
Give some of what you earned away, on purpose.

tracks.name: Selling
tracks.line: One thing to one person, to a real product.

steps.test: Sell one thing to one person.
Say what it is and what it costs, in one sentence.
Sell something to three people in one day.
Run a stall with real money and real change.
Hear no five times and keep going.
steps.note: Selling is mostly hearing no. The ones who are good at it stopped minding.

steps.test: Ask somebody what they were actually looking for, before offering anything.
Sell to ten people you have never met.
Work out what a thing costs you before you price it.
Price something so it sells, and defend the price when asked.
Put the price up and find out what happens.
Write down what you sold and what you made.
Handle somebody being unhappy with what you sold, and put it right.
Say no to a sale that would not have been fair.
Get somebody to buy a second time.
Ask a customer why they bought it, and listen.
Change what you sell because of what they told you.
Sell something you made yourself.
Get somebody to recommend you to somebody else.
Make something strangers buy more than once.
Teach somebody else to make their first sale, and let them do the talking.

tracks.name: Running something
tracks.line: A plan on paper to being asked back.

steps.test: Pick a small event you could actually run, a games afternoon for six children, say. Write down the five things it would need.
steps.note: Not a real event yet. The point is seeing the whole list before the day, which is most of running anything.

steps.test: Ask three people whether they would actually come.
Run one part of an outing yourself.
Make a list of everything that has to happen, in order.
Put a name against every item on that list.
steps.note: A job with no name against it does not get done. That is the whole of organising.

steps.test: Ask somebody to do one of them, and let them.
Set a date and tell people.
Work out what it costs before it starts.
Organise a small event for the group and make it happen.
Deal with one thing going wrong on the day.
Thank everybody who helped, by name.
Write down afterwards what you would change.
Run the same thing again, better.
Make an event cover its own costs with nobody topping it up.
Find out what people actually want first, then do that.
Run something where you were not the one at the front.
Hand a job to somebody who had never done it.
Cancel or change something when it was the right call.
Run something for people outside the group.
Run something people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: Making money grow
tracks.line: Saving to understanding it.

steps.test: Save for four weeks without spending any of it.
Say what you are saving for, out loud.
Put money somewhere you cannot get at it easily.
Explain what interest is, in your own words, correctly.
Work out what a pound a week becomes in a year.
Work out what it becomes in ten years with interest on top.
steps.note: This one sum has changed more lives than any other in this room.

steps.test: Save for three months without touching it.
Buy something, improve it, and sell it for more.
Do that twice and work out what you actually made.
Explain what a share in a company actually is.
Explain what a bank does with your money.
Say what inflation does to money in a tin under the bed.
Explain the difference between a debt that pays you and one that costs you.
Track a small investment for one month and explain what happened.
Watch it go down and not sell.
Track it for six months and explain what happened.
Say what you would never put money into, and why.
Spot something that was too good to be true, and walk past it.
Set aside a fixed share of everything that comes in, every time.
Teach a younger child what saving and interest mean.

tracks.name: Negotiating
tracks.line: Asking to a fair deal.

steps.test: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence.
Ask, and then stop talking.
steps.note: The silence after the ask does the work. Filling it is how people talk themselves down.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so you are both pleased.
Decide the number you will not go past, before you start.
Ask for a better price and get one.
Ask for something extra instead of money off.
Ask somebody what they need out of it, before saying what you want.
Ask a question instead of arguing back.
Get somebody to name their number first.
Say a number, out loud, and let it stand.
Walk away from a deal that was not good enough.
Go back the next day and get it anyway.
Find the thing that costs them little and is worth a lot to you.
Sort out a disagreement where both sides end up content.
Negotiate with somebody you will have to deal with again.
Give something away in a deal, on purpose, and say why.
Negotiate a bill or a subscription down, from your chair.
Say no and keep the relationship.
Negotiate something real on behalf of somebody else.
Become somebody people want to deal with again.

categories.name: Beauty and buildings
categories.line: Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.

tracks.name: Looking at buildings
tracks.line: Noticing, then being able to say why.

steps.test: Point at a building you think is pretty and one you think is ugly, and say which is which.
Say one reason why. Any reason counts, including a feeling.
Find two buildings on the same street and say which you would rather live in, and why.
Count the windows on a building and say whether they are evenly spaced.
Look at a building at eye level and say what a person walking past actually sees.
Find a building with a front door that looks like it means it.
Find one where the top, the middle and the bottom are clearly different.
Photograph three you like and three you do not.
Find one thing the three good ones share.
Find one thing the three bad ones share.
Walk somebody round and show them the good and the bad, and have them see it too.
Write down, in your own words, five rules for what makes a building good.

tracks.name: Proportion
tracks.line: Why some shapes feel right and others do not.

steps.test: Fold a piece of string exactly in half by eye, then check it.
Look at two rectangles and say which one feels nicer to you. There is no wrong answer.
Divide a line into three equal parts by eye, then measure and see how close you got.
Draw a square by eye and check it with a ruler.
Draw a house and put the door at a size that looks right for a person.
Measure a door, a chair and a step, and say what they all have in common.
steps.note: They are all sized off a human body. Almost everything that feels right is.

steps.test: Find something around you about one and a half times as long as it is wide.
Find something twice as long as it is wide, and say which shape you prefer.
Learn what the golden ratio is, roughly, and find one thing close to it.
Draw the same window three sizes and say which suits the wall.
Look at a room and say whether the ceiling is too low, too high, or right.
Find a building where one part is clearly the wrong size, and say which.
Draw a front of a building with everything in proportion to the door.
Space five windows evenly across a drawn wall, by eye.
Change one proportion in your drawing and see the whole thing change.
Draw the same building twice, once well proportioned and once badly.
Show both to somebody and see if they pick the same one you would.
Find a good proportion in something that is not a building at all.
Lay out a page, a poster or a garden using a proportion on purpose.
Draw the front of a building where every part looks right beside every other part.

tracks.name: Shapes and geometry
tracks.line: Circles, squares, tiles and solids.

steps.test: Find a circle, a square and a triangle in the room you are in.
Draw a circle freehand that somebody else agrees is properly round.
Draw a square and check its corners against the corner of a page.
Draw a triangle with all three sides the same, using a compass.
Make a shape that tiles, and fit six of them together with no gaps.
Find out which regular shapes tile and which cannot.
Step a compass around a circle six times and have it close exactly on itself.
Cut and fold paper into a solid shape that stands up.

tracks.name: Symmetry and pattern
tracks.line: Repeats, mirrors, and why they calm a room.

steps.test: Fold paper, cut a shape, open it out, and see the two halves match.
Find three symmetrical things around you.
Find something almost symmetrical and say what spoils it.
Draw the missing half of a face or a building so both sides match.
Make a pattern that repeats six times without a mistake.
Make one that repeats by turning instead of by mirroring.
Find a repeating pattern somewhere in your town.
Find a symmetrical building and a lopsided one, and say which feels calmer.
Find a building that is symmetrical on purpose except in one place.
Design a tile of your own.
Repeat it in every direction and fix whatever does not line up.
Design a tile that still works when you repeat it in every direction.

tracks.name: Arches and columns
tracks.line: The old ways, and why they were used.

steps.test: Find an arch somewhere near you and stand underneath it.
Build an arch out of blocks that stands up on its own.
Take the middle stone out and watch what happens.
steps.note: That is the keystone. Nothing holds until it is in, and everything holds once it is.

steps.test: Point out the three parts of a column — the base, the shaft and the top.
Say in your own words why an arch holds more weight than a flat beam.
Find a round arch and a pointed one and say which is older.
Find a column, an arch and a dome all in one day.
Explain to somebody younger why old buildings were built this way.

tracks.name: Your own town
tracks.line: Reading the place you actually live.

steps.test: Walk down your street and count the buildings you like.
Find the oldest building near you and say what is different about it.
Find out what your street was before it was houses.
Find a place where two different times sit side by side.
Draw a map of one street with the good buildings marked on it.
Find a spot in your town that feels good to stand in.
Say what makes it so — the width, the light, the noise, the edges.
Find a spot that feels bad to stand in, and say what would fix it.
Find where people naturally stop and stand, and say why there.
Find the one thing you would change about your town if you could change one.
Tell somebody who could do something about it.
Take somebody round and show them the town the way you now see it.

categories.name: The classical mind
categories.line: Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.

tracks.name: Spotting a bad argument
tracks.line: Telling a good argument from a loud one.

steps.test: Notice somebody changing the subject instead of answering, and say so afterwards.
Say what is wrong with "everybody does it, so it must be fine".
Say what is wrong with "he is wrong because he is an idiot".
Tell the difference between a reason and a feeling, in one argument.
Say what somebody would have to show you to change your mind.
steps.note: If nothing could change your mind, it was never an argument. It was a loyalty.

steps.test: Spot an argument that attacks the person instead of the point.
Spot one that says a small thing must lead to a disaster.
Spot one where somebody argues against a thing nobody said.
Spot three different bad arguments in a week and write down what was wrong with each.
Name five kinds of bad argument and give a real example of each.
Find a bad argument on your own side.
Say what you actually believe and what your reason is, separately.
Say back somebody else's argument so well that they agree that is it.
Then say why you still disagree.
Notice a number being used to prove something it does not prove.
Notice when something is true and irrelevant.
Point one out kindly, in the moment, without making anybody feel small.
Lose an argument on purpose because the other person was right.
Hold two possible answers open for a whole week without settling.
Teach somebody younger how to tell a good argument from a loud one.

tracks.name: Asking the good question
tracks.line: The Socratic habit, at any age.

steps.test: Ask why three times in a row about the same thing and see where you end up.
Ask somebody what a word really means, and keep going until it is clear.
Take a word like fair or brave and give an example and a non-example.
Ask a question you genuinely do not know the answer to.
Ask one that cannot be answered yes or no.
Ask a question and wait five full seconds for the answer.
steps.note: Most people fill the silence in two. The answer that was coming never arrives.

steps.test: Ask somebody how they came to think that.
Ask questions for five whole minutes without giving your own opinion once.
Ask the question everybody is avoiding.
Ask a question that helped somebody work something out themselves.
Change your own mind out loud, because of an answer somebody gave you.
Run a question with a group and keep everybody talking.

tracks.name: The big questions
tracks.line: Philosophy, done out loud, from about five upwards.

steps.test: Say what you think the word good means, in your own words.
Answer this and give a reason: is it ever right to tell a lie?
Say what you think fair means, and give a case where it is hard.
If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? Say why.
Say whether you are the same person you were at five, and why.
Argue properly for the opposite of what you actually believe.
Say what you would do in a case where both choices are bad.
Say whether something can be beautiful if nobody ever sees it.
Say what you think a good life is, in three sentences.
Ask an older person the same question and listen to all of it.
Read a page of a philosopher and say one thing you agreed with and one you did not.
Read a second one who disagrees with the first.
Say which of them you think is right, and what it would take to be sure.
Sit with a question for a whole week without answering it.
Write a page on what you believe and why.
Have somebody take it apart, and thank them.
Change one line of it, honestly.
Discuss a big question with somebody much younger, at their level.
Notice one of these questions turning up in an ordinary day.
Run a proper discussion for the group and let the best answer win, even if it is not yours.

tracks.name: The great stories
tracks.line: Myths, fables, and the books people keep reading.

steps.test: Listen to a whole myth or fable and say what happened.
Say what the story was actually about, underneath the events.
Say what the person in it wanted, and what stopped them.
Learn one myth well enough to tell it.
Tell it from memory to somebody else.
Read three of Aesop and say what each one is for.
Find a fable that you think is wrong.
Read a whole book that people have been reading for hundreds of years.
Say why you think people kept reading it.
Find the same idea turning up in two different old stories.
Find one turning up in something made this year.
Read a story from a place you know nothing about.
Learn the names of five gods or heroes and what each stood for.
Say which character in an old story you are most like, and why.
Read a second old book, longer than the first.
Argue that an old story got something wrong.
Tell an old story to somebody who has never heard it.
Read one aloud to the younger ones, doing the voices.
Read the same story again a year later and notice what changed.
Give somebody a book that mattered to you, and talk about it after.

tracks.name: Words and where they come from
tracks.line: Latin and Greek, the useful way.

steps.test: Learn what one word root means and find two English words that use it.
steps.note: Aqua means water: aquarium, aqueduct. That is the whole exercise, with a root of your own.

steps.test: Learn three roots.
Learn five roots.
Find a word in the room that uses one of them.
Learn ten roots and what they mean.
Learn five prefixes — un, re, pre, sub, trans.
Learn five endings and what they do to a word.
Break a long word into its parts and guess what it means.
Work out a long word you have never seen before, from its parts alone.
Do that with five words in one day.
Learn twenty Latin or Greek words and use them correctly.
Find where three English words came from, and be surprised by one.
Find two words that look related and are not.
Learn the Latin or Greek behind five things in a hospital or a courtroom.
Read one line of Latin or Greek and say what it means.
Read a motto on a building or a coin and translate it.
Learn thirty roots.
Guess a word in another European language from its root, and be right.
Explain to somebody why a word means what it means.
Teach somebody to break a long word into its parts.

tracks.name: One beautiful thing a day
tracks.line: Looking on purpose, and keeping what is worth keeping.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing today and say why it is.
Find one that nobody else would have noticed.
Do it every day for a week.
Write each one down.
Find one in something ordinary — a tool, a doorway, a pavement.
Find one made by a person, and one not made by anybody.
Do it every day for a month and write each one down.
Start a commonplace book and copy the first thing worth keeping into it.
Keep it for a month.
Learn one piece of music, one poem or one painting well enough to describe it from memory.
Show somebody something beautiful they had been walking past for years.
Read back a month of your own list and pick the best one.

tracks.name: Thinking on your own
tracks.line: A walk, a question, and no screen.

steps.test: Walk or sit for ten minutes with nothing to look at, thinking about one thing.
Say afterwards what you worked out.
Do it three times in one week.
Go for a walk with no phone at all.
Sit for twenty minutes with one question and nothing else.
Write down what you actually think about something, a page of it.
Write it without looking anything up first.
steps.note: Find out what you think before you find out what everybody else thinks. It is much harder afterwards.

steps.test: Read what somebody else thinks about it, after.
Write a page every week for a month.
Change your mind on paper, and write down what changed it.

Do it every morning for a week.
Do it on a day you did not want to.
Sit still for twenty minutes with somebody else in the room.
Do it every morning for a fortnight.
Notice one thing it has changed about an ordinary day.
Do it every morning for thirty days.
Sit for half an hour, once.
Lead five minutes of stillness for a group.

tracks.name: Attention
tracks.line: One task to deep work.

steps.test: Do one thing for ten minutes with nothing else going on.
Put the phone in a different room first.
Do one thing for twenty-five minutes without stopping.
Notice yourself drifting and come back, on purpose, five times.
Write down what you will do before you start, in one line.
Finish the thing you started before starting another.
Do two twenty-five minute stretches in one morning.
Work for an hour with no screen near you.
Notice the moment you want to check something, and do not.
Do the hardest thing on your list first.
Work with the notifications off, for a whole session.
Do a whole morning of one thing.
Read something difficult for forty minutes without stopping.
Notice what actually pulls you away, and write down the top three.
Remove one of those three from the room.
Work at the same time on three days in one week.
Do a whole morning of one thing, three weeks running.
Do something boring all the way to the end.
Notice one thing you can now do that you could not concentrate on before.
Explain to somebody else how you get yourself to concentrate.

tracks.name: Sleep
tracks.line: Going to bed to running your own rest.

steps.test: Go to bed without a fight, three nights running.
Go to bed without a fight, seven nights running.
Get up at the same time three days running.
Get up at the same time seven days running.
Notice how you feel after a bad night, and say so.
Keep screens out of the last half hour before bed, for a week.
Keep screens out of the last hour before bed for two weeks.
Get daylight on your face in the first hour of the morning, every day for a week.
Find out how many hours you actually need, by trying it.
Have the same last twenty minutes every night for a fortnight.
Run your own bedtime with nobody reminding you, for a month.
Explain what sleep does, and help somebody else fix theirs.

tracks.name: Doing hard things
tracks.line: Not giving up to choosing the hard one.

steps.test: Finish something you wanted to give up on.
Keep going for ten minutes after it stopped being fun.
Do something you have been putting off for a week.
Do the hard thing first thing in the morning.
Try something you are bad at, in front of other people.
Be the worst in the room and stay.
Ask for help with something you are ashamed of not knowing.
Fail at something publicly and go back and do it again.
Do the same hard thing three days running.
Finish something on a day you felt like nothing.
Choose the harder of two options on purpose, and say why.
Do something cold, or early, or uphill, on purpose.
Say yes to something that frightened you.
Keep a promise to yourself that nobody else knew about.
Start again after giving up on something once.
Do a hard thing for a month without missing more than two days.
Notice something that used to be hard and is not now.
Turn down the easy option in front of somebody.
Sit with something uncomfortable instead of fixing it straight away.
Help somebody else through the moment they want to quit.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: One thing to a habit.

steps.test: Say one good thing about today, out loud, at tea.
Do it three days running.
Do it every day for a week.
Say one that is about a person, not a thing.
Thank somebody properly, to their face, for something specific.
Thank somebody who is never thanked for it.
Find something good on a day that was bad.
Write down three each night for a week.
Write a thank-you letter that somebody keeps.
Do the daily one for thirty days.
Read back a month of them.
Start it at a table where nobody was doing it.

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.line: Twelve hours to thirty-six, without drama.
tracks.warn: Adults only past step five. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, underweight, still growing, on medication that needs food, or have ever had trouble with eating. Children stop at step four — going without snacks is theirs; going without meals is not.

steps.test: Eat nothing between your meals for one whole day.
steps.note: Meals only. No picking, no snacks. Most people have never once done this.

steps.test: Do that on three separate days in one week.
Drink a glass of water when you think you are hungry, and wait ten minutes.
steps.note: Half the time it was thirst. You will be surprised how often.

steps.test: Finish eating by eight in the evening, three nights running.
Go twelve hours with nothing but water. Sleep counts for most of it.
steps.note: Eight in the evening to eight in the morning. Almost everybody has done this by accident.

steps.test: Do twelve hours on three separate days in one week.
Push your first meal to midday. Fourteen hours, water only.
steps.note: From here on this ladder is for adults. See the note at the top.

steps.test: Do fourteen hours twice in one week.
Do sixteen hours, water only.
Do sixteen hours and get through an ordinary day inside it.
Sit through one wave of hunger without eating, and time how long it lasted.
steps.note: Time it properly. Hunger comes in waves and goes again, usually inside twenty minutes. Knowing that is most of the skill.

steps.test: Do sixteen hours on three separate days in one week.
Do eighteen hours, water only.
Do eighteen hours and take a walk inside it.
Do twenty hours.
Do twenty-four hours — one evening meal to the next evening meal.
steps.note: Water, and salt in it if you feel light-headed. Stop if you feel genuinely unwell; stopping is not failing.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours on a normal working day, not a quiet one.
Do twenty-eight hours.
Do thirty-two hours, and sleep through part of it.
Do thirty-six hours, and break it properly with a real meal.
steps.note: Break it small and slow — broth, eggs, something cooked. Not a feast. Breaking it badly is the part people get wrong.

categories.name: Creating order
categories.line: Clear it, mend it, give it away, clean the forgotten places. A life flows when the place is in order.

tracks.name: The bedroom
tracks.line: Where the day starts and ends.

steps.test: Clear every surface in the bedroom and put back only what you used this week.
Make the bed properly every morning for a week.
Empty the box by the door: bin it, give it, or find each thing a real home.
Get everything off the floor.
Clean the bedroom to a close look: under the bed, the skirting, the corners, the light switch.
Wash the bedding, the pillow covers, and the curtains or blind.
Take out anything that is not for sleeping or dressing.
Sit in the finished room for ten minutes with nothing in your hands and notice how it feels.

tracks.name: The desk
tracks.line: One clear surface to think at.

steps.test: Clear the desk to bare wood, wipe it, and put back the three things you use every day.
Every loose paper into one pile, then through it once: bin, file, or act on it today.
Sort the drawers: one drawer for what you use, everything else out.
Tame the cables: unplug what is not used, coil and label the rest.
Put one thing on it that you are glad to look at.
Sit down and check the chair and the screen are at the right height.
Set the desk each evening for the morning: a clear surface and one thing ready. Do it for a week.
Work a whole session at the clear desk and notice the difference.

tracks.name: The wardrobe
tracks.line: Only clothes you are glad to put on.

steps.test: Take every piece of clothing out and put it on the bed. All of it.
Try on anything you are unsure about. Keep only what fits now and what you are glad to wear.
Bag the rest today: give it, sell it, or bin what is worn out.
Put back what stays so you can see every piece at once.
Mend, or take to be mended, anything kept with a button, a hem or a zip gone.
Put the out-of-season things somewhere else entirely.
Work out what you are actually missing, and write the list.
Dress for a week from the finished wardrobe and count how many mornings were quicker.

tracks.name: Broken things
tracks.line: Fix it or let it go.

steps.test: Walk the whole house with a notebook and list every broken thing.
Fix three small things from the list today.
For each thing you will not fix, decide today: bin it, or take it to be repaired this week.
Take the ones for repair out of the house.
Fix one thing that needs a part or a tool: order the part, get the tool, do it.
Fix something you have walked past for a year.
Replace what has to be replaced, rather than leaving the gap.
Fix or remove the last thing on the list.
Notice one thing that broke because it was never maintained.
Do the one maintenance job that would stop it happening again.
Fix something for somebody else in the house.
Keep a page for broken things and clear it every Sunday for a month.

tracks.name: Giving away
tracks.line: What no longer serves you can serve somebody.

steps.test: Fill one bag with things you have not used in a year. Today.
Take it to a charity shop, a friend, or a giving box the same day.
Do the kitchen: gadgets, mugs, tins past their date. One bag out.
Do the books, games and hobby things you have finished with. Pass them on.
Do the bathroom cupboard and the medicine box.
Do the shed, the garage or the loft corner you avoid.
Give away one thing that is good and that you like, to somebody who will use it more.
Ask each person in the house to fill one bag too.
Sell one thing rather than keeping it "just in case".
Let go of one thing you kept only because it cost money.
Keep the bag by the door and add to it for a fortnight.
A month on, count what you missed.

tracks.name: The phone and the inbox
tracks.line: The clutter you carry in your pocket.

steps.test: Delete every app you have not opened in a month.
Delete the screenshots and the junk photos from the last month.
Unsubscribe from twenty emails you never read.
Turn off every notification that is not a person talking to you.
Get the inbox to empty once: archive, delete, or act.
Clear the home screen to one page of what you use.
Put the two apps that eat the most time off the first page.
Back up the photographs you would be sick to lose.
Sort one year of photographs and delete the near-duplicates.
Cancel one subscription you had forgotten you pay for.
Check where you are still signed in, and sign out of what you do not use.
Keep the inbox at empty by the end of each day for a week.

tracks.name: The forgotten places
tracks.line: Behind, under, on top of, and inside.

steps.test: Clean the windows, inside and out, in one room.
Wash or wipe the blinds and the curtain rail.
Clean behind and under the sink, and the bin itself.
Empty and wipe the fridge, shelf by shelf, and bin what is past.
Clean the oven, or the thing in the kitchen you have been avoiding.
Wash the curtains, or take them to be cleaned.
The top of the cupboards, the light shades, and the skirting all the way round: one room.
Move the furniture and clean what was under it.
Clean the front door, the handle and the step.
Do the one place in the house nobody has looked at in years.
Descale, empty or change the filter on something that needed it.
Do one forgotten place every week for a month.

tracks.name: Keeping it
tracks.line: Order that stays.

steps.test: Everything you own has a home: choose one for the five things that never get put away.
Put those five things away in their homes tonight.
Ten minutes every evening putting the day back. Do it for three days.
Do it for a week.
Clear one surface every single evening for a week.
One in, one out: for a week, nothing new comes in without something going.
One in, one out for a month.
A Sunday reset: half an hour that puts the whole place right. Do one.
Do four of them, one a week.
Put things away where they live rather than where they will do.
Stop a pile before it starts, three times in one week.
Walk the whole house with a close look. Where has clutter crept back? Deal with it today.
Find the one spot that always goes wrong, and change what it is for.
Get everybody in the house to keep one shared surface clear for a week.
Deal with the post the day it arrives, for a fortnight.
Leave a room right when you leave it, every time, for a week.
Keep the place in a state you are glad to walk into for a month.
Do a reset after something disrupted it — illness, visitors, a bad week.
Notice that putting things away has stopped needing a decision.
Keep the place in a state you are glad to walk into for three months.

tracks.name: Your own things
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Shoes, cover, clothes, books, and one box put right.

steps.test: Put your shoes side by side by the door, the same way round.
Hang your coat up on a hook.
Pull the cover up straight on your bed when you get out of it.
Put your clothes in the wash basket at bedtime, without being asked.
Put the books back on the shelf the right way up.
Put the lids back on the pens and the tops back on the tubs.
Empty one box of toys onto the floor and put every single one back in.
Find a home for one thing that never had one.
Put away what you were playing with before the next thing comes out.
Do that for a whole afternoon.
Tidy your room with somebody, and stay until it is finished.
Do all of it one whole day without anybody reminding you.

journey.name: Easy wins
journey.line: Every one of these is a decision rather than a skill. Minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to learn first. Most people are surprised they had never done them.

journey.name: Courage, worth and asking
journey.line: Deliberately early. Once you can ask for things, walk into anywhere and hear no without flinching, a great many things that looked like they cost money turn out not to. This stage quietly changes what everything after it is worth.
